explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. God says, “Woe to the shepherds of Israel, who only feed themselves!” Then He asks, “Should not the shepherds feed their flock?” (Ezekiel 34:2) Feeding the flock is the whole job, so a shepherd who only feeds himself is a one-man party with a LOT of guests missing.
The poor never come up in these verses, friend. God's complaint is aimed at the shepherds themselves. He says they “only feed themselves.” That is what the verse says, and it is the whole charge.

Nice try, but lambs aren't named in this verse. The shepherds' job is to feed their flock, and God says they “only feed themselves.” Nobody in that picture is getting fed except the shepherds. Hey, even I share my dough with the whole counter.

True. God says, “You eat the fat, wear the wool, and butcher the fattened sheep.” That's eating, wearing and butchering, and the sheep get nothing out of any of it. The verse ends, “…but you do not feed the flock.”

It's actually true, friend. God tells the shepherds, “You eat the fat, wear the wool, and butcher the fattened sheep.” They take from the flock and the sheep get nothing back. The verse ends, “…but you do not feed the flock.”

That's the one. God says, “You have not strengthened the weak, healed the sick, bound up the injured, brought back the strays, or searched for the lost.” That's five jobs on the list, and none of them got done. Five! I can barely keep up with ONE oven, and these shepherds skipped the whole list.

Close to the list, but not on it. The verse says the shepherds have not “strengthened the weak.” The care was for the weak ones, and the strong aren't what God names here. The one that fits the blank is the sick.
The young aren't on this list, friend. God names the weak, the sick, the injured, the strays and the lost. The one that fits the blank is “healed the sick.” Those are the ones who were left alone.

Right. God says, “Instead, you have ruled them with violence and cruelty.” (Ezekiel 34:4) A shepherd is supposed to care for sheep, and this is the opposite. I think this one hurts to read, so take a breath with me. The good news is that God doesn't leave it there.

Bribes and flattery aren't mentioned in this passage. The verse says plainly, “you have ruled them with violence and cruelty.” It's a hard line, and I think it's meant to be. Still, God has more to say about it, and it's good.

Rules aren't what God points to here. He says the shepherds “ruled them with violence and cruelty.” That is a heavy line, and I think it's heavy on purpose. God isn't done talking, though, and what comes next is a comfort.

explanations.answer: They become food for wild beasts
explanations.explanation: Yes. God says, “They were scattered for lack of a shepherd, and when they were scattered they became food for all the wild beasts.” (Ezekiel 34:5) A flock with no shepherd is in real trouble. That's a heavy picture, and I think it shows why God cares so much.

explanations.answer: They are sold at the market
explanations.explanation: A market never comes up in these verses. God says the scattered sheep “became food for all the wild beasts.” (Ezekiel 34:5) It's a sad line, friend. A flock with no shepherd is a flock in danger.

explanations.answer: They wander back to the fold
explanations.explanation: The sheep don't wander back here. God says they were “scattered for lack of a shepherd” and “became food for all the wild beasts.” (Ezekiel 34:5) He also says there was “no one to search for them or seek them out.” (Ezekiel 34:6) A lost sheep needs a shepherd to come get it.
It's the other way around, friend. God says the flock was scattered “with no one to search for them or seek them out.” (Ezekiel 34:6) Nobody went looking. That's the charge against these shepherds.

False, and you read it right. God says the flock was scattered “with no one to search for them or seek them out.” (Ezekiel 34:6) The sheep are on the mountains and the hills, and nobody goes after them. That's exactly why God steps in later.

explanations.answer: Remove them from tending the flock
explanations.explanation: That's right. God says, “I will demand from them My flock and remove them from tending the flock, so that they can no longer feed themselves.” They lose the job. A shepherd who only feeds himself doesn't get to keep the staff.

explanations.answer: Give them a bigger flock to tend
explanations.explanation: A bigger flock would be a prize, friend, and this isn't one. God says, “I will demand from them My flock and remove them from tending the flock.” They lose the flock they had. Nobody's getting a promotion here.

explanations.answer: Send them out to find the strays
explanations.explanation: God doesn't send these shepherds out to look. He says He will “remove them from tending the flock.” The searching is something He takes on Himself: “Behold, I Myself will search for My flock and seek them out.” (Ezekiel 34:11)

True. God says, “For I will deliver My flock from their mouths, and it will no longer be food for them.” He pulls the sheep out of the danger. The flock was being treated like a meal, and God says that's over.
It's true, friend. God says, “For I will deliver My flock from their mouths, and it will no longer be food for them.” He steps in and rescues the sheep. That's one promise you can count on.
YES. God says, “Behold, I Myself will search for My flock and seek them out.” The shepherds didn't search, so the LORD does it Himself. He doesn't send anybody else.

Ezekiel is the prophet God speaks to in this passage, and his job is to deliver the message. He isn't the one who goes looking. God says, “Behold, I Myself will search for My flock and seek them out.” The search belongs to the LORD.
The elders of Israel aren't named in this promise. God says, “Behold, I Myself will search for My flock and seek them out.” He doesn't hand the job to anybody. The LORD takes it on Himself.

That's it. God says, “I will bring them out from the peoples, gather them from the countries, and bring them into their own land.” They get gathered from everywhere they were scattered. Then He brings them home.
A temple isn't in this verse, friend. God says He will “bring them into their own land.” The flock gets gathered out of the countries and brought home. The word that fits the blank is land.

No fortress here. God says He will “gather them from the countries, and bring them into their own land.” Then He feeds them “on the mountains of Israel, in the ravines, and in all the settlements of the land.” This flock gets a homecoming, not a hideout.

It's the other way around, friend. God says, “I will seek the lost, bring back the strays, bind up the broken, and strengthen the weak; but the sleek and strong I will destroy.” His care goes to the lost and the weak. Then He adds, “I will shepherd them with justice.”

False, and nicely read. God says, “I will seek the lost, bring back the strays, bind up the broken, and strengthen the weak; but the sleek and strong I will destroy.” His care goes to the ones the old shepherds ignored. That's what He means by shepherding “with justice.”

That's the word. God asks, “Is it not enough for you to feed on the good pasture? Must you also trample the rest of the pasture with your feet?” It's one thing to eat. It's another to wreck what's left for everybody else.

Sharing would be lovely, friend, but it isn't what these sheep do. God asks, “Must you also trample the rest of the pasture with your feet?” They eat the good grass and then stomp the rest. I'd call that the opposite of sharing.

These sheep aren't guarding anything. God asks, “Is it not enough for you to feed on the good pasture? Must you also trample the rest of the pasture with your feet?” The leftover pasture gets trampled. The word that fits is trample.

Horns it is. God says, “Since you shove with flank and shoulder, butting all the weak ones with your horns until you have scattered them abroad.” The weak ones are pushed right out. I think that's what makes God's coming judgment such good news for them.

Close, but this verse says horns. God says they shove “with flank and shoulder, butting all the weak ones with your horns until you have scattered them abroad.” They're pushing the weak ones around until they're gone. Teeth never come into it.

A tail can swish, but it can't butt anybody. The verse says they shove “with flank and shoulder, butting all the weak ones with your horns until you have scattered them abroad.” So the word is horns. The weak ones get pushed out.
It's the opposite, friend. God says, “I will save My flock, and they will no longer be prey.” (Ezekiel 34:22) The flock that was food for the beasts gets rescued. That's the promise.

False, and that's the good part. God says, “I will save My flock, and they will no longer be prey. I will judge between one sheep and another.” The flock that was hunted gets saved. And God takes care of the bullying sheep too.

That's the one. God says, “I will appoint over them one shepherd, My servant David, and he will feed them.” David was a shepherd boy before God chose him as Israel's king (1 Samuel 16:11-13). So a shepherd feeding the flock is a good name to hear.

Moses, the man God sent to bring Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 3:10), is a great name. But this verse names someone else. God says, “I will appoint over them one shepherd, My servant David, and he will feed them.” The answer is David.

Joshua, who took over leading Israel after Moses (Joshua 1:1-2), is a great name too. But God doesn't say it here. He says, “I will appoint over them one shepherd, My servant David, and he will feed them.” The name in this verse is David.

True. God says, “I will make with them a covenant of peace and rid the land of wild animals, so that they may dwell securely in the wilderness and sleep in the forest.” The wild beasts that once hunted the flock are gone. Then the sheep are safe, even in the wilderness.

It's actually true, friend. God says, “I will make with them a covenant of peace and rid the land of wild animals.” The beasts that once threatened the flock are cleared out. Then the sheep can dwell securely.

Blessing is right. God says, “I will send down showers in season—showers of blessing.” The rain comes right on time, and it brings good things. Fruit on the trees and produce from the land follow in the next verse.
No sorrow in this picture, friend. God says, “I will send down showers in season—showers of blessing.” The rain is good news for the flock. The word that fits is blessing.
Not warning. In this new picture God says, “I will send down showers in season—showers of blessing.” The rain comes in its season and the land gives its fruit. The word that fits is blessing.

True. God says, “Then they will know that I am the LORD, when I have broken the bars of their yoke and delivered them from the hands that enslaved them.” He breaks the yoke Himself. And they come to know who He is.
It's true, friend. God says He will break “the bars of their yoke” and deliver them “from the hands that enslaved them.” He does the breaking Himself. The flock walks out free.

That's the one. God says, “Then they will know that I, the LORD their God, am with them, and that they, the house of Israel, are My people.” After all that scattering, the flock hears that God is with them. I think that's the line to hold onto.
Nowhere does God say He needs their help. He does the searching, the rescuing and the feeding Himself. What the flock will know is this: “I, the LORD their God, am with them.” That's the answer.
This verse says the opposite, friend. God says, “Then they will know that I, the LORD their God, am with them.” He doesn't move on from His flock. He is with them.
Yes. God says, “You are My flock, the sheep of My pasture, My people, and I am your God.” He gives them a name and says whose they are. It's a warm way to close the chapter.
No soldiers here, friend. God says, “You are My flock, the sheep of My pasture, My people, and I am your God.” After a whole chapter of scattered sheep, He calls them His people. That's the answer.
Guests is a nice word, but it's not the one in this verse. God says, “You are My flock, the sheep of My pasture, My people, and I am your God.” So the word is people. They're His, and He says so.
